source: NCERT Class IX, Democratic Politics I, Polity Ch. 5.

sections.heading: 1. Why Rights are Needed
points: **Rights** = reasonable claims of persons recognised by society and **sanctioned by law**.
Rights protect **minorities from the majority** and citizens from the **misuse of government power**.
Some rights are placed in the Constitution as **Fundamental Rights** — the government cannot take them away.

sections.heading: 2. The Six Fundamental Rights
points: **Right to Equality** — equality before law; no discrimination; abolition of untouchability.
**Right to Freedom** — speech, assembly, movement, residence, profession; personal liberty.
**Right against Exploitation** — bans forced labour, child labour and human trafficking.
**Right to Freedom of Religion** — freedom to follow, practise and propagate any religion.
**Cultural and Educational Rights** — minorities can preserve their culture and run institutions.
**Right to Constitutional Remedies** — the right to approach the courts if rights are violated.

sections.heading: 3. Right to Constitutional Remedies
points: Called by **Dr Ambedkar** the **'heart and soul' of the Constitution**.
Citizens can go to the **Supreme Court or High Courts** to enforce their rights.
The courts can issue **writs** (habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo warranto).
The **National Human Rights Commission (NHRC)** also protects rights.

sections.heading: 4. Rights Widen Over Time
points: The scope of rights has widened — e.g. **Right to Information (RTI, 2005)**, and the **Right to Education (RTE)** made a fundamental right (Article 21A).
Rights come with **duties and reasonable restrictions**.
Rights are the foundation of a **democracy**.

sections.heading: 5. High-Yield One-Liners (Last-Minute Recall)
points: Six Fundamental Rights: Equality, Freedom, against Exploitation, Freedom of Religion, Cultural & Educational, Constitutional Remedies.
Right to Constitutional Remedies = 'heart and soul' of the Constitution (Ambedkar).
Courts enforce rights via writs (habeas corpus, mandamus, etc.).
Right against Exploitation bans forced labour, child labour, trafficking.
RTI (2005) and Right to Education (Article 21A) widened rights.

sections.heading: 6. Common Traps (Watch Out)
points: There are **six** Fundamental Rights (the Right to Property was removed as a fundamental right by the 44th Amendment, 1978).
The **Right to Constitutional Remedies** is the 'heart and soul' (Ambedkar) — it makes other rights enforceable.
The **Right against Exploitation** bans **forced/child labour and trafficking**.
**RTE (Article 21A)** made education a fundamental right.
